The National Director-General of the Obidient-Kwankwaso Movement, John Ughulu, speaks with DARE AKOGUN on the movement’s criticism of the Nigeria Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council W hy did you criticise the NDC’s election preparedness a day after it unveiled its presidential campaign council? There is no better time to speak the truth than when circumstances demand it. My concern is that the unveiling of NDC’s Presidential Campaign Council is coming rather late, particularly given the enormous political challenges we face and the strength of the opposition we are preparing to confront. This is not about attacking the party or undermining its leadership. It is about expressing a genuine concern for the success of our collective political project. A party seeking to challenge an incumbent government must approach an election with strength, urgency, strategic discipline and a clear sense of direction. We cannot afford to be reactive or constantly play catch-up. We must be proactive, set the pace and dictate the direction of the campaign rather than allow the opposition to determine the terms of engagement. Campaign strategy is not just about appointing people to positions. It is about identifying the right people, building structures, mobilising the electorate, establishing effective communication channels and preparing early enough to execute a winning strategy. Timing is critical. My concern is that the NDC must not give the impression that it is lagging in its preparations. Nigerians who are looking for a credible alternative deserve a party that demonstrates preparedness, competence and the capacity to lead from the front. I believe the NDC can do better, and that is precisely why I am speaking out. Constructive criticism should not be mistaken for hostility. We must be willing to confront uncomfortable truths and correct weaknesses before they become costly mistakes. What should the party have done earlier to show readiness for 2027? Failure to plan is a plan to fail. I strongly believe that if the NDC intends to make a meaningful impact in the 2027 general elections, it should have developed, strategised and implemented its policies, procedures and campaign plans long before now. The decision of the Independent National Electoral Commission to move the election timetable forward was not something the NDC should have ignored when planning its electoral strategy. The party should have anticipated the need for adequate preparation and inaugurated its Presidential Campaign Council much earlier. That would have provided sufficient time to identify weaknesses, make necessary internal corrections, strengthen its structures and ensure that all critical aspects of the campaign were properly coordinated. An election of this magnitude cannot be won on ambition alone. It requires preparation, strategic thinking and timely execution. Why should the party make an already challenging political journey more difficult through avoidable delays? Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources Let me emphasise that this is my personal opinion, borne out of genuine concern for the NDC’s preparedness and its prospects in the 2027 elections. My intention is not to undermine the party but to challenge its leadership to recognise that winning an election requires more than political enthusiasm. You suggested that 90 per cent of those appointed to the council may still need the OK Movement’s structure. Who are these people and why are you confident? The OK Movement is not another conventional political movement built on rhetoric, empty promises or the familiar political practices Nigeria has experienced for decades. We are a movement founded on a clear ideology, defined principles and a genuine commitment to changing the political direction of our country. The foundation of this movement dates back to August 25, 2025, following our visit to former President Olusegun Obasanjo to seek clarity on the direction of our country. We were concerned about the economic hardship, political instability and national decline confronting Nigeria. We believed the country needed a new political direction driven by competence, integrity, equity, justice and responsible leadership. From the beginning, we understood that meaningful political change could not be achieved through social media popularity, political declarations or the accumulation of prominent names alone. It required organisation, strategic planning and deliberate investment in grassroots mobilisation. This is why we maintained that many individuals appointed to the Presidential Campaign Council will eventually need to engage with the OK Movement to strengthen their grassroots mobilisation. We understand the structures we have built, the people who sustain them and the mobilisation capacity we are developing. We respect experience and recognise the political contributions of those appointed. However, respect for political experience must not prevent us from asking legitimate questions about capacity, competence and preparedness. A presidential campaign council is not constituted simply to produce an impressive list of names. It must be a strategic instrument for winning elections. The real test is not how many prominent names appear on its list, but how effectively it can mobilise voters, protect the integrity of the electoral process and deliver victory at the polls. 2027: Atiku, Makinde near alliance deal 2027: Gombe APC targets one million votes for Tinubu 2027: Tompolo urges Anambra voters to back Tinubu The NDC leadership has stated that the campaign council is a party affair. Why are you meddling? I am sure you support a particular football team, even if you have never contributed a single penny to its development or management. Yet, as a fan, you have every right to criticise the players, manager, coach and even the club’s management when they fail to meet expectations. Support does not mean accepting failure, and loyalty does not mean remaining silent in the face of poor performance. The same principle applies to politics. The OK Movement supports the NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, because we believe in their principles, ideology, integrity, competence and commitment to building a better Nigeria. However, our support for them does not mean we have surrendered our right to question the leadership of the NDC. We support the candidates because of what they represent, not because we have given the party leadership a blank cheque to do as it pleases. If the leadership acts in ways that contradict the principles of responsibility, discipline, transparency, competence and accountability, we have every right to express our concerns and offer constructive criticism. We cannot claim to be fighting for a better Nigeria while turning a blind eye to practices that contradict the values we seek to promote. The OK Movement is not in politics to flatter leaders, endorse mediocrity or applaud every decision simply because it comes from a political party we support. Our loyalty is to the principles that brought us together, our commitment is to the Nigerian people and our support for the NDC ticket is rooted in our belief in Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso. Are your public criticisms not divisive and demarketing to the party? Supporting a political party does not mean abandoning independent thought. Constructive criticism is not disloyalty; it is a demonstration of responsibility. If we want a government that will be accountable to the people, we must first be willing to demand accountability from those seeking our support. The OK Movement will support, mobilise, campaign and defend the votes for the NDC candidates. But we will not abandon our principles, compromise our values or surrender our right to speak the truth. At this critical stage of our political journey, we cannot afford to confuse political prominence with electoral capacity or the number of appointments with organisational strength. Are you still part of the NDC, or are you running a parallel campaign structure? I believe we have long moved beyond that narrative. There is a clear difference between a misunderstanding and a disagreement. When my intentions are misunderstood, my position can easily be misinterpreted. It is therefore important to distinguish between the two before concluding. The OK Movement fully understands the principle of party supremacy. Despite being an independent organisation, we maintain the utmost respect for the NDC leadership and recognise the party’s position in the political process. However, our independence is equally important. We have every right to organise, constitute and promote our own presidential campaign council in pursuit of our objectives and commitment to the 2027 general elections. Our independence should not be misconstrued as hostility, just as our respect for the party should not be interpreted as a surrender of our identity or autonomy. Our position is clear. It is time to move beyond unnecessary narratives and focus on the bigger picture: mobilising support, securing votes and defending the mandate of our candidates. The OK Movement has moved on from this matter, and we encourage everyone to do the same. Our focus remains on the mission ahead. What will the OK Movement do if the NDC ignores your concerns? The OK Movement remains confident that the NDC represents a far better option for the average Nigerian and offers a credible opportunity to deliver the change our country urgently needs. We remain fully committed to working collaboratively with the party, bringing our strength, organisational capacity and mobilisation network to bear wherever necessary to achieve our shared objectives. Our mission is clear: to work together, mobilise Nigerians, strengthen our collective efforts and secure victory at the polls in 2027. We believe that through unity of purpose, strategic collaboration and a shared commitment to the Nigerian people, we can achieve the desired outcome and build a better future for our country. Dare Akogun
